summary: This document defines TEAP version 1, a tunnel-based EAP method that uses TLS to build a mutually authenticated tunnel. Inside it, TLV objects carry authentication and other data. It obsoletes RFC 7170 and updates RFC 9427.

plainLanguage.summary: TEAP is a way for a device to log in to a network. It first makes a secure encrypted tunnel using TLS, in the same way a web browser sets up a secure connection to a website. Inside that tunnel it runs the actual login, which might be a password, a certificate, or an older login method. The tunnel also proves that both ends took part, so a third party cannot slip in the middle.

subtitle: A standards-track EAP method that builds a TLS tunnel, then runs password, certificate or other logins inside it.

tldr.problem: Existing tunnel-based EAP methods such as PEAP, EAP-TTLS and EAP-FAST are vendor-specific or informational, yet the industry wanted a Standards Track tunnel-based EAP method.
tldr.mechanism: TEAP first uses a TLS handshake to build a protected tunnel (Phase 1). In Phase 2 the peer and server exchange TLV objects inside the tunnel to run one or more inner authentications, then bind them to the tunnel with a cryptographic check and end with a protected result.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9930 obsoletes RFC 7170 and updates RFC 9427. It documents what running implementations actually do, and it states that only a small set of inner methods is known to interoperate fully.

today: RFC 9930 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2026. It obsoletes RFC 7170 and updates RFC 9427. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document itself notes that only a small set of inner methods is known to interoperate, and that the fixes belong to a future TEAPv2.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A tunnel-based Extensible Authentication Protocol method is an EAP method that establishes a secure tunnel and executes other EAP methods under the protection of that tunnel. It can be used in any lower-layer protocol that supports EAP authentication.

Several existing tunnel-based EAP methods use TLS to establish the secure tunnel. These include Protected EAP, EAP Tunneled Transport Layer Security, and EAP Flexible Authentication via Secure Tunneling. However, they are all either vendor-specific or informational, and the industry calls for a Standards Track tunnel-based EAP method. This document describes TEAP version 1, which is based on EAP-FAST. The changes from EAP-FAST are largely minor, made in order to meet the requirements listed for a standard tunnel-based EAP method.

The document also defines cryptographic derivations for use with TLS 1.2. When TLS 1.3 is used, the definitions in the separate TLS 1.3 EAP document MUST be used instead. TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 have been deprecated, so the definitions given here apply only to TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.

The document contains substantial changes from RFC 7170, largely clarifications and corrections to that specification. There is one major change: the cryptographic-binding information was interpreted differently by each implementation. The implementations are interoperable, but only for a subset of the functionalities described in RFC 7170. This specification describes how TEAPv1 works in theory and also explains what subset of TEAPv1 is currently interoperable, with all interoperability issues documented separately from the normal protocol operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Several login methods already build a secure tunnel and run the real login inside it, but they are either vendor-specific or only informational. TEAP is the standards-track version of that idea, and this document replaces the earlier TEAP specification with a clarified one that also records what real implementations actually agree on.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
TEAP authentication occurs in two phases after the initial EAP Identity request and response exchange. In the first phase, TEAP employs the TLS handshake to provide an authenticated key exchange and to establish a protected tunnel. Once the tunnel is established, the second phase begins with the peer and server engaging in further conversations to establish the required authentication and authorization policies. TEAP makes use of TLV objects to carry out the inner authentication, results and other information, such as channel-binding information.

The architectural model shows four logical entities: the peer, the authenticator, the TEAP server and the inner method server. The TEAP server is the backend authentication server, and the inner method server handles the application data, that is, the inner methods, EAP, passwords and so on, inside the TLS tunnel. These are logical entities and may or may not correspond to separate network components. Typical IEEE 802.11 deployments place the authenticator in an access point while a RADIUS server may provide the TEAP and inner method server components.

The layering model puts the pieces in order. TEAP packets are encapsulated within EAP, and EAP in turn requires a transport protocol. TEAP packets encapsulate TLS, which is then used to encapsulate user authentication information. At the top sit the inner EAP method and other TLV information, then the TLV encapsulation layer, then TLS, then TEAP itself, then EAP, and at the bottom the carrier protocol, which may be EAP over LAN, RADIUS or Diameter.

TLVs may be both inside and outside the TLS tunnel. Outer TLVs are optional TLVs outside the tunnel, allowed only in the first two messages in the TEAP, the first server-to-peer message and the first peer-to-server message. Inner TLVs are sent within the tunnel. In Phase 1, Outer TLVs help establish the TLS tunnel and no Inner TLVs are used. In Phase 2, TLS records may encapsulate zero or more Inner TLVs, but no Outer TLVs are used.
sections.plainLanguage: TEAP has four logical roles: the device logging in, the thing it logs in through, the TEAP server, and the server that handles the inner login. They can all sit in one box or be spread across several. The nesting is simple: the inner login sits in TLV objects, which sit in TLS, which sits in TEAP, which sits in EAP, which rides on something like RADIUS.

sections.title: Phase 1: Tunnel Establishment
sections.content:
TEAP relies on the TLS handshake to establish an authenticated and protected tunnel. The TLS version offered by the peer and server MUST be TLS version 1.2 or later. The implementation MUST support the cipher suites TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256. Other cipher suites MAY be supported, and the recommended cipher suites for TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 MUST be implemented. Anonymous cipher suites such as TLS_DH_anon_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA may only be used when the inner method provides mutual authentication, key generation and resistance to on-path and dictionary attacks. Cipher suites that do not provide confidentiality MUST NOT be used.

Use of TLS-PSK is NOT RECOMMENDED. TEAP has not been designed to work with TLS-PSK, and no use cases, security analyses or implementations have been done.

The EAP server initiates the TEAP conversation with an EAP request containing a TEAP/Start packet. This packet includes the TEAP start bit, the TEAP version, and an authority identity TLV. The TLS payload in the initial packet is empty. The authority identity TLV gives the peer a hint of the server's identity, which may help the peer select the right credential. The conversation continues with the peer sending an EAP-Response packet of EAP type TEAP with the start bit clear and the negotiated version. This message encapsulates one or more TLS handshake messages. When the full TLS handshake is performed, the first payload of TEAP Phase 2 MAY be sent along with a server-finished handshake message, to reduce the number of round trips.

TEAP implementations MUST support mutual peer authentication during tunnel establishment using the cipher suites named above. The peer does not need to authenticate as part of the TLS exchange but can alternatively be authenticated through additional exchanges carried out in Phase 2.

The version is negotiated in the first exchange. The server sets the version field to the highest it supports, and the peer answers with that version if it supports it, or with its own highest version if it only supports a lower one. If the peer only supports higher versions, it sends an EAP-Nak to negotiate a different EAP type. Because the version is not protected by TLS, the peers MUST exchange the version number they received during negotiation inside the Crypto-Binding TLV, and the receiver MUST check that it matches.
sections.plainLanguage: Phase 1 is an ordinary TLS handshake, with the server proving who it is with a certificate. The version of TEAP is agreed in the very first message, and the two ends later repeat that version inside the protected part of the conversation, so nobody can quietly downgrade the protocol on the way.

sections.title: Phase 2: Tunneled Authentication
sections.content:
The second portion of the TEAP authentication occurs immediately after successful completion of Phase 1. Phase 2 occurs even if both peer and authenticator are authenticated in the Phase 1 TLS negotiation. Phase 2 MUST NOT occur if the Phase 1 TLS handshake fails, because the tunnel has not been established successfully. Phase 2 consists of a series of requests and responses encapsulated in TLV objects. Phase 2 MUST always end with a Crypto-Binding TLV exchange and a protected termination exchange.

If the peer is not authenticated in Phase 1, it SHOULD send one or more Identity-Hint TLVs as soon as the TLS connection has been established, so that the server can choose an authentication type appropriate for that identity. Without the hint, the server does not know which inner method the peer supports and must choose one and propose it, which the peer may reject, in which case the peer fails to authenticate and fails to obtain network access.

The TLV exchange includes the execution of zero or more inner methods within the protected tunnel. A server MAY proceed directly to the protected termination exchange without performing any inner authentication if it does not wish to request further authentication from the peer. A server MAY request one or more authentications within the tunnel, and after each inner method completes it decides whether to begin another or to send a Result TLV. Implementations MUST support at least two sequential inner methods, which allows both machine and user authentication to be performed. Implementations SHOULD limit the number of sequential inner authentications.

Where several inner methods are used, implementations SHOULD order them so that a method that derives an Extended Master Session Key is used first, before any other method, because this helps to tie the inner method to the TLS session securely. Implementations SHOULD support both EAP and basic password authentication for inner methods, and implementations that support multiple types of inner methods MUST support all of those methods in any order or combination. A server can request user authentication and receive machine authentication instead, and if the server is configured to accept machine authentication it MUST accept that response.

The completion of each inner method is signalled by an Intermediate-Result TLV. Where that TLV indicates failure, an Error TLV SHOULD also be included using the most descriptive error code possible. When all inner methods have completed, the server MUST send a Result TLV indicating success or failure instead of a TLV that carries an inner method.
sections.plainLanguage: Phase 2 is the real login, run inside the tunnel. The server can ask for one or more inner logins in a row, such as a machine login and then a person login, and the peer may answer with a different inner method than the one requested. Whatever happens, the exchange ends with a Result TLV saying success or failure, and that result is protected.

sections.title: Message and TLV Formats
sections.content:
TEAP packets are framed like other EAP packets, with the fields transmitted from left to right in network byte order. The Code field is one octet and is 1 for a Request and 2 for a Response. The Identifier field is one octet and aids in matching responses with requests; it MUST be changed on each Request and MUST match in the Response. The Length field is two octets and gives the length of the EAP packet, with octets outside that range treated as data link layer padding and ignored on reception.

The Type field is 55 for TEAP. The Flags field carries five bits: L for the presence of the four-octet Message Length field, M for more fragments, S for a TEAP Start message sent by the server, O for the presence of the four-octet Outer TLV Length field, and R, which is reserved and must be zero. The Ver field is 3 bits and holds the protocol version, and this document describes version 1. The Message Length field and the Outer TLV Length field are each four octets and are present only when their flag bit says so. The TLS Data field, when present, consists of an encapsulated TLS packet in TLS record format.

TLVs are the objects that carry data inside the tunnel. Each TLV begins with a mandatory bit M and a reserved bit R, then a 14-bit TLV Type, then a two-octet Length giving the length of the value in octets, then the value itself. Twenty types are allocated, from 0 Unassigned through 19 Identity-Hint. If a peer or server receives a TLV that is not of the correct format, the TLV MUST be discarded.

The mandatory bit tells the other end whether support is required. If a peer or server does not support a TLV marked mandatory, it MUST send a NAK TLV in the response, and all the other TLVs in the message MUST be ignored. An unsupported TLV marked optional can simply be ignored. If all TLVs in a message are marked optional and none are understood, a Result TLV SHOULD be sent to the other side in order to continue the conversation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each TEAP packet has a small header with the type, a version, and flags for length and fragmentation. Inside it, the data is a list of TLV objects, each with a type number, a length and a value. A TLV can be marked as one the other end must understand, in which case an unknown one makes the whole message fail.

sections.title: Limitations and Interoperability of TEAPv1
sections.content:
TEAPv1 implementations are limited in functionality compared with what the protocol is theoretically capable of. These limitations mean that only a small number of inner methods are fully supported by existing implementations. The interoperability issues are limited to the use and derivation of the Compound MACs, which are derived from the inner MSK and EMSK. In short, implementations are known to derive different values for the Compound MACs when more than one inner method provides an EMSK.

The document lists which inner methods are known to work. EAP-MSCHAPv2 and EAP-TLS are known to work on their own, for both user and machine credentials. EAP-MSCHAPv2 followed by EAP-MSCHAPv2, and EAP-TLS followed by EAP-MSCHAPv2, are known to work in any order of user and machine credentials. EAP-MSCHAPv2 followed by EAP-TLS, and EAP-TLS followed by EAP-TLS, are known to work when both the supplicant and the authenticator ignore the EMSK Compound MAC field.

The main reason is that the most well-known TEAP supplicant supports only EAP-MSCHAPv2 and EAP-TLS for the inner methods, does not encode the EMSK Compound MAC field in all of the Crypto-Binding TLVs it sends, and ignores that field in all of the Crypto-Binding TLVs it receives. The known authenticator implementations support this client, but any other combination of inner methods was not tested. As a result, each authenticator implemented entirely different derivations of the EMSK Compound MAC field, due to both the complexity of the cryptographic derivations and the lack of interoperability testing. This difference was discovered only after multiple implementations had been shipping for years.

Any attempt to change TEAPv1 to address these issues would likely result in one or more implementations being non-compliant with the updated specification, and would result in multiple incompatible versions of TEAPv1. That approach is not acceptable. In the interest of maintaining known interoperability, the specification documents these issues rather than trying to correct the problem. Since both the TEAP message and the Crypto-Binding TLV contain a Version field, the better path forward is to publish this specification while documenting the large caveats for TEAPv1. Any changes to TEAP can then be done in a future TEAPv2 specification.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the catch. In practice only a couple of inner methods are known to work together, because the implementations disagreed about how to compute one of the checks. Fixing the text now would break the software already in the field, so the document records the problem instead and leaves a proper fix for a future version.

sections.title: Crypto-Binding and Key Derivation
sections.content:
For key derivation and crypto-binding, TEAP uses the Pseudorandom Function and MAC algorithms negotiated in the underlying TLS session. The implementation needs a way to determine the version and cipher suite in use, and can then work out which PRF and MAC algorithm to use.

With TEAPv1, the TLS master secret is generated as specified in TLS, or obtained from the session ticket mechanism when resumption is used. TEAPv1 makes use of the TLS Keying Material Exporters to derive the session key seed, with no context data used in the export process. That seed is used by the Phase 2 conversation both to bind the inner methods to the tunnel and to generate the resulting TEAP session keys.

The Crypto-Binding TLV is used to prove that both the peer and the server took part in the tunnel establishment and in the sequence of authentications. It also provides verification of the TEAP type, the version negotiated and the outer TLVs exchanged before the tunnel was established. It must be accompanied by an Intermediate-Result TLV indicating success, and it must be exchanged and validated before any Intermediate-Result or Result TLV value is examined, whether or not there was an inner method. If it fails to validate for any reason, that is a fatal error.

The TLV is 76 octets long. It carries a version octet, a Received-Ver octet that must be set to the TEAP version received during version negotiation, a four-bit Flags field saying which compound MACs are present, a four-bit Sub-Type field distinguishing a binding request from a binding response, a 32-octet nonce, and the two compound MAC fields, each 20 octets. The nonce is a 256-bit value that is temporally unique and is used for compound MAC key derivation at each end. The nonce in a request MUST have its least significant bit set to zero, and the nonce in a response MUST have the same value as the request nonce except that the least significant bit MUST be set to one.

After each successful inner EAP authentication, the EMSK and/or MSK are cryptographically combined with key material from Phase 1 to generate a compound MAC key, and the Compound MAC is the first 20 octets of the MAC over a buffer. That buffer is built by concatenating, in order, the whole Crypto-Binding TLV with both MAC fields zeroed out, the EAP type sent by the other party in the first TEAP message, which must be TEAP and is encoded as one octet of 0x37, all the outer TLVs from the first message the server sent to the peer, and all the outer TLVs from the first message the peer sent to the server. Because both sides use the same outer TLVs in the opposite order, any modification to the outer TLVs in transit is detected.

The final MSK and EMSK are generated from the final, that is, the n-th, inner method, as part of the key hierarchy, using the TLS PRF with the secret S-IMCK[n]. The EMSK is typically only known to the peer and the server and is not provided to a third party. If no inner method has created an MSK or EMSK, both are generated directly from the session key seed.
sections.plainLanguage: The Crypto-Binding TLV is the proof that both ends really took part. It carries a random nonce and two 20-octet checks that combine the tunnel's keys with the keys the inner login produced. Both sides build the same buffer from the same pieces, so if anyone changed anything on the way, the checks will not match.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TEAP is designed with a focus on wireless media, where the medium itself is inherent to eavesdropping. In wired media an attacker would have to gain physical access to the wired medium, whereas wireless media enables anyone to capture information as it is transmitted over the air, enabling passive attacks. Physical security cannot be assumed, and security vulnerabilities are far greater. The threat model used for the security evaluation of TEAP is the one defined in EAP.

As a whole, TEAP provides message and integrity protection by establishing a secure tunnel for protecting the inner methods. The confidentiality and integrity protection is defined by TLS. The integrity of the key generating inner methods executed within the tunnel is verified through the Crypto-Binding TLV, which ensures that the tunnel endpoints are the same as the inner method endpoints. Where server unauthenticated provisioning is performed, TEAP requires that the inner provisioning method provide for both peer and server authentication.

As is true for any negotiated EAP, the EAP NAK messages used to suggest an alternate authentication method are sent unprotected and are subject to spoofing. During unprotected method negotiation, NAK packets may be interjected as active attacks to bid down to a weaker form of authentication. Both the peer and the server should have a method selection policy that prevents them from negotiating down to weaker methods. Inner method negotiation resists attacks because it is protected by the mutually authenticated TLS tunnel. Selection of TEAP as an authentication method does not limit the potential inner methods, so TEAP should be selected when available.

Separation of the TEAP Phase 1 from the Phase 2 conversation is NOT RECOMMENDED. Allowing the Phase 1 conversation to be terminated at a different server than the Phase 2 conversation can introduce vulnerabilities if there is not a proper trust relationship and protection for the protocol between the two servers. The vulnerabilities named are loss of identity protection, offline dictionary attacks, lack of policy enforcement, and on-path active attacks. There may be cases where a trust relationship exists between the Phase 1 and Phase 2 servers, such as on a campus or between two offices within the same company, in which case a proxy solution without end-to-end protection of TEAP MAY be used.
sections.plainLanguage: TEAP was designed for wireless networks, where anyone nearby can overhear. TLS supplies the confidentiality and the Crypto-Binding check proves both ends were the same on both sides of the tunnel. Two things to watch: the outer negotiation is unprotected, so a downgrade to a weaker method is possible, and splitting the tunnel server from the inner login server is not recommended unless the two trust each other completely.

viz.caption: THE SHAPE OF A TEAP CONVERSATION

messages.label: EAP-Request (TEAP/Start)
messages.note: Carries the version and an Authority-ID TLV hint.

messages.label: EAP-Response (TLS ClientHello)
messages.note: The first TLS handshake message, inside the EAP frame.

messages.label: TLS handshake completes
messages.note: The server proves its identity with a certificate. Phase 1 ends here.

messages.label: EAP-Response (Phase 2 TLVs)
messages.note: The inner authentication runs inside the tunnel.

messages.label: EAP-Response (Result TLV)
messages.note: Success or failure, protected by the Crypto-Binding TLV.

messages.label: EAP-Success
messages.note: The cleartext EAP result must match the protected one.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: Mandatory bit. 0 for an optional TLV, 1 for a mandatory one.

fields.name: TLV Type
fields.desc: The type of the TLV. Twenty types are allocated, from 0 Unassigned to 19 Identity-Hint.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: The length of the Value field in octets.

items.label: Unassigned
items.desc: Not used.

items.label: Authority-ID
items.desc: A hint of the server's identity.

items.label: Identity-Type
items.desc: A hint of the type of identity to use.

items.label: Result
items.desc: Success or failure of the protected termination.

items.label: NAK
items.desc: A mandatory TLV was not supported.

items.label: Error
items.desc: Describes an error to the other party.

items.label: Channel-Binding
items.desc: Carries channel binding information.

items.label: Vendor-Specific
items.desc: Carries a vendor's own data.

items.label: Request-Action
items.desc: Asks the peer to take an action.

items.label: EAP-Payload
items.desc: Carries an inner EAP exchange.

items.label: Intermediate-Result
items.desc: Reports the outcome of one inner method.

items.label: PAC
items.desc: Deprecated.

items.label: Crypto-Binding
items.desc: Binds the inner methods to the tunnel.

items.label: Basic-Password-Auth-Req
items.desc: Asks for a username and password.

items.label: Basic-Password-Auth-Resp
items.desc: Carries the username and password.

items.label: PKCS#7
items.desc: Carries a PKCS#7 object.

items.label: PKCS#10
items.desc: Carries a certificate signing request.

items.label: Trusted-Server-Root
items.desc: Carries trusted server roots.

items.label: CSR-Attributes
items.desc: Attributes for a certificate signing request.

items.label: Identity-Hint
items.desc: A hint about the peer's identity.

items.text: All the outer TLVs from the first message the peer sent to the server.
